name: Losada Vinos de Finca Mencía Bierzo Altos de Losada La Bienquerida
text:
## Losada Vinos de Finca Mencía Bierzo Altos de Losada La Bienquerida

Your listing has no vintage, so I've covered the wine across vintages. Where a score applies to one year, I name it. My rating at the bottom is for the 2022, the current release.

**The region.** Bierzo ([satellite](https://www.google.com/maps?q=El+Bierzo,+Ponferrada,+Spain&t=k)) is a small mountain basin in León province, in Spain's north-west. It is a small denomination made up of little plots of old Mencía and Godello vines, where small-scale, artisanal grape growing is the norm.

**The producer.** Losada Vinos de Finca was set up in 2004 just outside the village of Pieros, on the Camino de Santiago, halfway between Cacabelos and Villafranca del Bierzo, facing the ruins of Castro Ventosa, a Roman-era fortification. Look at [Pieros](https://www.google.com/maps?q=Pieros,+Cacabelos,+Spain&t=k), [Castro Ventosa](https://www.google.com/maps?q=Castro+Ventosa,+Cacabelos,+Spain&t=k), [Cacabelos](https://www.google.com/maps?q=Cacabelos,+Leon,+Spain&t=k) and [Villafranca del Bierzo](https://www.google.com/maps?q=Villafranca+del+Bierzo,+Leon,+Spain&t=k) from above.

The architect Jesús Manzanares took the wall around the nearby Roman fort as his inspiration for the winery building. The early wines were made in rented premises, and the new winery opened in 2011. Losada's stated angle is clay. They looked for old Mencía vineyards on mostly clay soils, a terroir the 1990s Bierzo newcomers had largely passed over in their rush toward slate.

**The vineyard.** La Bienquerida is a vineyard planted in 1906. It was close to disappearing when Losada rescued it, and since 2018 it has carried "vino de paraje" (single-site) certification for Las Chas, in Cacabelos. Here is [Las Chas](https://www.google.com/maps?q=Las+Chas,+Cacabelos,+Spain&t=k) from above.

**The grapes.** Mencía dominates. Like many old sites, the vineyard is a mixed planting of Mencía, Merenzao, Doña Blanca, Pan y Carne and Palomino. The 2022 is listed as 95% Mencía and 5% other grapes, with 4,260 bottles made. The grapes are fully destemmed, macerated for 30 days and fermented with wild yeasts. The wine then spends 15 months in foudres and 500-litre French oak, and it is bottled without filtration or cold stabilisation.

**What the critics say.** The most recent scores come from James Suckling's team. They gave the 2022 and the 2021 95 points each. Earlier scores are 94 from Suckling for the 2019 and 91 from Peñín for the 2018. The 2015 has 92 from Peñín and 96 from Suckling, the 2012 has 91 from Parker and 94 from Peñín, and the 2008 has 91 from Parker and 93 from Peñín.

Tim Atkin MW also reviewed the 2022. I could see his note but not his score. He describes a wine that is powerful but composed, with a slaty, iron-tinged mineral core, and he gives it a window of 2024-34. Suckling's reviewer stresses chalky minerality, firm tannins and freshness. He says it is very drinkable now but can also age.

There is one dissenting voice. Amaya Cervera of Spanish Wine Lover gave the 2015 16 out of 20. She found ripe, dark fruit and slightly bitter tannins, a touch of warmth, and a wine that needed time to open.

**Community notes.** I couldn't reach CellarTracker notes for this wine. The nearest equivalent I found is on Delectable. The 2011 vintage there averages 9.16 from users and 9.33 from trade professionals.

**Where to buy in Canada.** I don't know of a listing in BC, Alberta or Ontario.

**Practical note.** At this point the 2022 can be drunk now or kept for about eight more years. Because the wine is unfiltered, decanting and giving it some air before serving is recommended. About an hour is a good start, served at 16 °C. For food, go with roast lamb, game, or Bierzo's own smoked pork sausage, botillo.

**Curious aside: clay versus slate.** Mencía grown on clay tends to have plumper, thinner skins, so the structure is gentler and the wines usually feel softer. La Bienquerida sits on a mix of slate and clay. That helps explain why critics describe it as both firm and fresh, a step up in grip from Losada's clay-led wines.

**From the history books**
- **About 1st century BC to 1st century AD:** Castro Ventosa, the hill fort opposite the winery, is a major Roman-era site, and it shaped the winery's design. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:Search?search=Castro+Ventosa&go=Go)
- **1906:** The La Bienquerida vines were planted. That was within a generation of phylloxera sweeping Europe's vineyards, which means this old field blend is a living record of how Bierzo replanted. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:Search?search=Phylloxera&go=Go)
- **Middle Ages to today:** The winery sits on the Camino de Santiago, the pilgrim route to Santiago de Compostela. Pilgrims have walked past these vineyards for centuries. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:Search?search=Camino+de+Santiago&go=Go)
